source_note: Topic structure follows the AQA GCSE English Language specification. Connections, sequence and prerequisites are expert-authored teaching relationships (exam boards do not publish these).

Section B: Writing — descriptive or narrative writing

Section B: Writing — present a viewpoint

AO5–AO6: Writing — communicate clearly and accurately

connections.why: The reading AOs (identify, interpret, analyse, evaluate) are exactly the skills Paper 1 fiction reading is marked against
The same reading skills transfer to non-fiction, with added focus on comparing viewpoints
Creative writing is assessed on AO5 (content/organisation) and AO6 (technical accuracy)
Viewpoint writing applies the same AO5/AO6 craft to a persuasive, audience-aware task
Close reading of a fiction writer's techniques models the methods students reuse in their own descriptive writing
Analysing how writers build a viewpoint feeds directly into constructing one's own argument
Both papers build the core analytical reading skill; fiction first, then the harder comparison of non-fiction perspectives
Descriptive control of language and structure underpins the more rhetorical demands of viewpoint writing
The spoken-language AOs are the criteria the NEA presentation is judged against
A presentation is followed by spontaneous Q&A, testing adaptive spoken response
The presentation is the context in which candidates demonstrate spoken Standard English
Standard English must be sustained even in the unscripted question phase
Constructing a written viewpoint and structuring a spoken presentation share the same persuasive, audience-aware skills
Clear written communication and confident spoken delivery draw on the same command of register and structure
